steps.name: make the change
steps.instructions: Make the change the request asks for, and only that, in the files it needs, following how this project already does things. Code and test files may both change here. When the request is a reviewer's thread, implement what the reviewer asked for: the structure or behaviour the thread names (a factory, a class, a check, a rename), not a smaller stand-in for it (a private method where a factory was asked for). Every reply counts, and the person's own reply in the thread (or their answer under it) is the decision ("yes, a reusable factory class"). Put new code where this project keeps code of that kind: find where its existing code of that kind lives (grep for a few of them) and follow that folder, naming and registration, not the file the comment is on. When the change alters behaviour, add or adjust the test that proves it. When it changes no behaviour (a refactor, an extract into a helper, a rename, test code only), write no new test (the existing tests passing is the proof) and end with one line "NO-BEHAVIOUR-CHANGE: <what changed>". Never write a test that reads source code as text. Run the tests you touched before you stop. If the change cannot be tested (a text, a comment), end with one line "UNTESTABLE: <why>". When it is bigger than the request (a new page, a migration, the API contract, several parts), stop and say so: it needs the small or the feature flow.

steps.name: check: does it do what the reviewer asked?
steps.instructions: Lens: intent. Compare the uncommitted change (git diff HEAD, and the new files git status lists) with what was asked: the reviewer's thread in the request, every reply in it, and the person's answer when there is one (the person's own reply is the decision). Read only the changed files and, to judge where code belongs, a few files of the same kind in this project. Blocking, one line each, starting with "Does not do what the reviewer asked:", then what was asked and what the change does instead: the change builds a different or smaller thing than the structure or behaviour the thread names (a private method where a factory class was asked for, a rename where an extraction was asked for); or it puts the new code where this project does not keep code of that kind (name where it does). Nothing else is blocking here: not style, not more than the thread asks. End with one line "INTENT: met — <what the change does, in one sentence>" or "INTENT: missed — <the reason>", then the BLOCKING line.
